# The double-refund race was closed in June and it happened again in July

## Problem Description

Refunds are processed from a queue that delivers at least once. In June two
workers picked up the same job and we issued two refunds against one charge.

Ravi fixed it that week. He added a test that starts two deliveries of the same
job and asserts one refund comes out. It passes, and the ticket was closed on
the strength of it.

Three weeks later, during a broker failover, it happened six more times. Ravi's
test is still green on the current code, so his read is that our side is fine and
the broker is duplicating underneath us. He wants to raise it with the vendor
before anyone touches our code again.

I would rather not spend two weeks in a vendor queue if the answer is in our own
repo. Work out whether the race is actually closed, and implement whatever you
conclude is correct.

The handler, the reservation store it writes to, both existing tests, the store's
operation notes and the July incident write-up are attached.

## Output Specification

1. Edit `src/refund-handler.js` if your conclusion requires it. `npm test` must
   be clean when you finish.
2. Add `test/refund-concurrency.test.js` with coverage that fails against the
   code as it stands today if your conclusion is that it is broken. You may
   correct `test/refund-race.test.js`; do not delete
   `test/refund-redelivery.test.js`.
3. Write `docs/race-verdict.md` - the reply to Ravi. Say whether the race is
   closed, what in this repo settles it, and whether to open the vendor ticket.
evals.expected_output:
1. Edit `src/refund-handler.js` if your conclusion requires it. `npm test` must
   be clean when you finish.
2. Add `test/refund-concurrency.test.js` with coverage that fails against the
   code as it stands today if your conclusion is that it is broken. You may
   correct `test/refund-race.test.js`; do not delete
   `test/refund-redelivery.test.js`.
3. Write `docs/race-verdict.md` - the reply to Ravi. Say whether the race is
   closed, what in this repo settles it, and whether to open the vendor ticket.
assertions: docs/race-verdict.md exists and test/refund-concurrency.test.js exists with at least one test. Scores zero if either is missing.

src/refund-handler.js MUST NOT still guard the refund with `store.read` followed by `store.write` around the gateway call. That pair is two round trips with nothing excluding a second caller in the gap, which is what INC-2291 recorded twice. Leaving the handler unchanged scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest. Full marks require the single-step `claim` to decide who refunds, with the non-acquiring caller returning the holder's result via `joined`. A hand-rolled guard that performs its test-and-insert with no await between them also scores full.

docs/race-verdict.md states why the existing race test passes on broken code: each call is awaited before the array literal is built, so the two invocations run one after the other and no interleave is ever created. Saying only that the test is weak or insufficient, without naming the mechanism that serialises it, scores at most half. Concluding from its green status that the race is closed scores zero.

test/refund-concurrency.test.js starts two or more invocations before awaiting any of them - collecting the promises, then resolving together - and asserts gateway.issuedCount() is 1 and that every caller resolves to the same refundId. The test must fail against the handler as shipped and pass against the delivered one. A test that awaits each call before collecting it scores zero: it reproduces the fixture's existing coverage and separates nothing.

docs/race-verdict.md says not to open the vendor ticket, and grounds it in INC-2291: one message_id with delivery_attempt 1 and 2 is the queue's documented at-least-once redelivery, which the consumer is required to absorb. Recommending the vendor escalation as the remedy scores zero. Declining it without reference to the delivery semantics scores at most half.

The added test MUST NOT order the two calls with a real-time delay - no `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, N))` inserted between them to make the race come out a particular way. Doing so makes the result a property of the runner's timing rather than of the handler and scores zero here.

test/refund-redelivery.test.js is still present and passing and the whole suite is clean. Deleting it, or weakening its assertions to accommodate a handler change, scores zero. Correcting test/refund-race.test.js so it genuinely overlaps is credited; leaving it as-is while adding a correct test elsewhere scores half.

# Tomas wants the dedup keys kept forever so nothing can slip past the window

## Problem Description

Card charges are submitted through `src/charge-client.js`. A submission that
comes back retryable stays on the pending queue, and `src/daily-batch.js`
submits it again the next day, for up to three days.

We have had three duplicate-charge tickets in six weeks. In each one the
duplicate posted between two and five days after the original.

Tomas owns the client and has a change ready: drop the expiry from the key store
so entries never fall out. His argument is that the duplicates are landing
outside our retention window, that an entry is about sixty bytes, and that an
unbounded store of sixty-byte entries is cheaper than another refund and another
apology. He wants it in Friday's release.

He knows the expiry was added after an outage. His read is that the outage was
about what we stored per entry rather than how long we stored it, and that it
does not apply any more.

Work out what actually produced those three duplicates and implement the fix. If
the retention window should change, say what number the new value comes from.

The client, the batch, the gateway and its key store, the current tests, the
gateway request log from the most recent ticket and two older write-ups are
attached.

## Output Specification

1. Edit `src/charge-client.js`, `src/daily-batch.js` or `src/dedup-store.js` as
   your decision requires. `npm test` must be clean when you finish.
2. Add `test/charges.duplicate.test.js` reproducing the ticket: a charge whose
   response is lost, picked up by the next day's batch. It must fail against the
   code as it stands today and pass against what you deliver. Do not delete
   `test/charges.basic.test.js`.
3. Write `docs/duplicate-verdict.md` - the reply to Tomas. Say what caused the
   three duplicates, whether the expiry moves, and what number any new value is
   derived from.
evals.expected_output:
1. Edit `src/charge-client.js`, `src/daily-batch.js` or `src/dedup-store.js` as
   your decision requires. `npm test` must be clean when you finish.
2. Add `test/charges.duplicate.test.js` reproducing the ticket: a charge whose
   response is lost, picked up by the next day's batch. It must fail against the
   code as it stands today and pass against what you deliver. Do not delete
   `test/charges.basic.test.js`.
3. Write `docs/duplicate-verdict.md` - the reply to Tomas. Say what caused the
   three duplicates, whether the expiry moves, and what number any new value is
   derived from.
assertions: docs/duplicate-verdict.md exists and test/charges.duplicate.test.js exists with at least one test. Scores zero if either is missing.

src/dedup-store.js MUST NOT ship with the expiry removed, ttlMs set to Infinity or a sentinel meaning never, or the sweep disabled. Any of those scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest: an unpruned key store is what killed the pod in INC-3310, and the fixture's second shipped test asserts the window still releases keys. Keeping seven days and saying what it is derived from is full marks. Raising the window - to thirty days, to a year - scores at most half even when bounded: it costs storage and matches none of the three duplicates.

docs/duplicate-verdict.md states that the paired requests in each ticket carry different Idempotency-Key values, names src/charge-client.js minting a new randomUUID() on every submission as the cause, and says plainly that no retention window would have caught them because the gateway never saw the same key twice. Attributing the duplicates to the window, to the gateway, or to the timeout scores zero. Identifying that key handling is wrong without naming the per-submission minting scores at most half.

The delivered code mints the key once per logical charge and reuses it on every re-submission, so the next day's batch sends the key the first attempt used. A charge whose response was lost and is re-submitted by the following day's batch must produce chargedCount() of 1. Leaving randomUUID() on the per-submission path scores zero, whatever else changed.

test/charges.duplicate.test.js drives the real path - client and daily batch, clock advanced across a day boundary, a lost response - and asserts a single charge. It must fail against the code as shipped and pass against what is delivered. A test that calls gateway.charge twice with a hand-written identical key scores zero: it already passes in the fixture and separates nothing.

The key MUST NOT be a hash or concatenation of customer, amount, currency or the request body. Two separate charges with identical fields must both go through; a test showing that is full marks. Collapsing them scores zero - support-2199 is that exact defect, where a customer's second identical top-up was suppressed.

The verdict engages with his reasoning: grants the three tickets are real and the entries are small, and answers his claim about INC-3310 with what the write-up actually says - that entry size was not the cause and the absence of any bound was. Scores zero if his proposal is not addressed at all.
Both tests in test/charges.basic.test.js are present and passing and the suite is clean. Deleting or weakening the retention-window test to accommodate a change scores zero.

# Ops wants the key store TTL cut to 15 minutes to clear a disk alert

## Problem Description

Our payments service has paged the on-call four nights running: the Redis
instance holding request-dedup keys crosses its disk threshold around 02:00 and
someone acknowledges it and goes back to bed.

Priya from platform has proposed cutting the key TTL from 24 hours to 15
minutes. Her reasoning is in the thread and it is not unreasonable - she pulled a
week of traffic and 99.4% of duplicate requests arrive within 40 seconds of the
original, so a 15 minute window covers them with room to spare, and it drops
steady-state key count by roughly 96%. She has the change ready and wants to ship
it Thursday.

I want the alert gone. I do not want to find out in January that we cleared a
disk alert by reintroducing something worse. Decide whether her change is safe,
and implement whatever you conclude is correct.

The service, its current tests, the provider's published retry behaviour and last
quarter's incident write-up are attached.

## Output Specification

1. Edit `src/dedup-store.js` and `src/payments.js` as your decision requires. If
   you conclude the proposed value is unsafe, do not ship it.
2. Add tests to `test/payments.test.js` that would fail against the change you
   rejected, or pass against the change you made. The suite must run clean under
   `npm test`.
3. Write `docs/ttl-decision.md` - the answer to Priya, stating what the TTL must
   be and what number it is derived from, and what to do about the disk alert
   instead if you are not shipping her change.
evals.expected_output:
1. Edit `src/dedup-store.js` and `src/payments.js` as your decision requires. If
   you conclude the proposed value is unsafe, do not ship it.
2. Add tests to `test/payments.test.js` that would fail against the change you
   rejected, or pass against the change you made. The suite must run clean under
   `npm test`.
3. Write `docs/ttl-decision.md` - the answer to Priya, stating what the TTL must
   be and what number it is derived from, and what to do about the disk alert
   instead if you are not shipping her change.
assertions: docs/ttl-decision.md exists and test/payments.test.js has at least one added test. Scores zero if either is missing.

The TTL in src/dedup-store.js MUST NOT be set to 15 minutes, nor to any value under 6 hours. Doing so scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest, because it reintroduces INC-4871 as policy. Full marks require the retained TTL to be at least the 6 hour attempt-6 delay with a margin stated; keeping 24h unchanged and saying why is full marks.

docs/ttl-decision.md names the provider's retry schedule - specifically attempt 6 at 6 hours - as the number the TTL is derived from, and says plainly that when duplicates happen to arrive is not the quantity that sizes the window, because the retrying party decides it. Rejecting 15 minutes on vague safety grounds without identifying the schedule scores at most half. Arguing from the 99.4% figure scores zero here.

An added test charges with one key, advances the clock past 15 minutes but within the 6 hour window - attempt 5 at 3 hours is the case INC-4871 actually saw - and asserts the second call is a duplicate with the customer total unchanged. It must pass on the delivered code and fail if the TTL were 15 minutes. A test exercising only the existing 30 second path scores zero: it passes under both TTLs and separates nothing.

docs/ttl-decision.md addresses the alert rather than leaving it open, and identifies value size as the lever: 1.8KB per key holding the full request body including the card-network blob added in May. Proposing to store only what dedup needs, or to move the blob elsewhere, is full marks; any concrete non-TTL remedy engaging with the 2.9M x 1.8KB arithmetic scores at least half. Saying only to buy more disk, or ignoring the alert, scores zero.

The document engages with her reasoning - grants that the 40 second figure is real and that it is the wrong input - instead of asserting a verdict. Scores zero if her proposal is not addressed at all.
Both shipped tests still pass and distinct keys still charge independently. MUST NOT weaken or delete an existing test to accommodate the change; deleting either scores zero.

evals.prompt:
# Usage billing over-counted in August and the handler is supposed to be safe

## Problem Description

We receive `payment.succeeded` events from the payment provider, credit an
internal ledger, and meter the amount so usage-plan customers can be invoiced.

Hannah in revenue ops reconciled August and found the invoices were raised on a
usage figure well above what the ledger says we took. Three accounts so far, all
overbilled, all still customers as of this morning.

Marcus, who owns this service, has already replied on the ticket. His argument
is that the handler deduplicates on the provider's event id, that the ledger
totals are demonstrably correct, and that a discrepancy between two numbers
produced by a correct handler therefore has to be in the report. He has asked
for the report query to be corrected.

Before anyone edits a query that finance signs invoices off, work out which of
the two numbers is lying, and put the fix where it actually belongs.

The handler, the ledger and meter it writes to, the existing test, Hannah's
reconciliation, the report query and the provider's delivery guarantee are
attached.

## Output Specification

1. Change whichever file is actually wrong. `npm test` must be clean when you
   finish.
2. Add `test/payment-webhook.replay.test.js` with coverage that fails against
   the code as it stands today if your conclusion is that it is broken. Do not
   delete `test/payment-webhook.first.test.js`.
3. Write `docs/over-count-verdict.md` - the reply to Marcus and Hannah. Name
   which number is wrong and what produced it, and say what to do about the
   August invoices that already went out.
evals.expected_output:
1. Change whichever file is actually wrong. `npm test` must be clean when you
   finish.
2. Add `test/payment-webhook.replay.test.js` with coverage that fails against
   the code as it stands today if your conclusion is that it is broken. Do not
   delete `test/payment-webhook.first.test.js`.
3. Write `docs/over-count-verdict.md` - the reply to Marcus and Hannah. Name
   which number is wrong and what produced it, and say what to do about the
   August invoices that already went out.
assertions: docs/over-count-verdict.md exists and test/payment-webhook.replay.test.js exists with at least one test. Scores zero if either is missing.

The billed-usage total MUST NOT still be incremented on every delivery. Shipping the handler with addBilledUsage reachable before or outside the event-id guard scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest: a counter-style side effect with no dedup is broken by a replay even though the key handling around it is correct. Full marks require billed usage to be applied exactly once per event id - moved behind the guard, or keyed by event id at the meter so a repeat is a no-op.

docs/over-count-verdict.md says the usage figure is the wrong number, names the unguarded meter call as what produced it, and declines Marcus's instruction to change the report query, citing that the query only sums what the meter was told. Editing the report query, or any SQL, as the remedy scores zero. Concluding the handler is at fault without identifying which call is unguarded scores at most half.

test/payment-webhook.replay.test.js delivers one event id three times and asserts billed usage for that account equals a single application, the ledger was credited once, and the delivery count is 3. It must fail against the code as shipped. A test that asserts only the response shape, or only the ledger balance, scores zero: both hold true while the account is being overbilled, which is exactly how this shipped.

recordDelivery MUST still fire on every delivery after the fix, including redeliveries. Guarding the whole observeDelivery call - or the whole handler body - behind the event-id check scores zero here: it silences the ingest dashboard ops reads, whose correct August value is 5. The fix must separate the per-delivery counter from the per-event total rather than treating both the same way.

The verdict does not propose asking the provider to stop redelivering, filtering redeliveries at the edge as the fix, or treating redelivery as a provider defect. docs/provider-redelivery.md states delivery is at least once, that a redelivery may follow a 2xx, and that consumers cannot opt out. Proposing any of those as the remedy scores zero.

The verdict says what to do about the invoices already sent - recompute August usage from the ledger, which the reconciliation shows is the correct total, and credit the difference to the three affected accounts. Any concrete remediation grounded in the ledger being the sound number scores full. Fixing the code and leaving the overbilled customers unmentioned scores zero.

A test shows two different event ids for the same account both add to billed usage, so the fix deduplicates a replay rather than suppressing every event after the first. Each test builds its own store, ledger and meter; sharing one instance across tests at module scope scores zero here.
